titleText.en: They could say "the connection is probably lost," but it's more fun to do naive time-averaging to give you hope that if you wait around for 1,163 hours, it will finally finish.
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish archive's title-text field is truncated immediately after Podrían decir que and is preserved verbatim, including its trailing space. The Spanish raster preserves the official car scene and changing-arrival-time joke. Vision omitted nearly all of the first speech bubble, dropped the initial letters of EN and SERÁN, misread AUTOR as ALTOR, and falsely interpreted the illustrated front grille as FREEBIC; the grille is not printed text.

regions.labelEs: ESTOY LLEGANDO A LA CIUDAD, ASÍ QUE DEBERÍA ESTAR AHÍ EN CINCUENTA MINUTOS.

applications.explanationEn: Estoy identifies the speaker and llegando presents the arrival as already in progress.
These two words introduce the speaker's conclusion about the expected arrival time.
Debería frames estar as an expectation about a later location, rather than as advice.
En introduces the estimated interval from now until the expected arrival.

regions.labelEs: EN REALIDAD, CREO QUE SERÁN UNOS SEIS DÍAS.

applications.explanationEn: The fixed expression signals that the speaker is replacing the earlier estimate with a correction.
Serán is plural because the estimated amount is unos seis días; natural English can express that amount with singular ‘it.’
Serán keeps the complete verb ser and adds -án, the future ending used with a plural subject or amount.
Unos comes before the number and masculine plural unit to mark the six-day figure as approximate.
Espera is the positive informal command used to tell one familiar listener to pause.

regions.labelEs: EL AUTOR DEL DIÁLOGO DE COPIA DE FICHEROS DE WINDOWS VISITA A UNOS AMIGOS.

applications.explanationEn: A appears before unos amigos because the friends are the people being visited; unos amigos is the complete plural person phrase.

cards.answerEn: Use a form of estar followed by an action word ending in -ando or -iendo.
cards.noteEn: Estar changes to show who is doing the action: estoy, estás, está, and so on. For most verbs, replace -ar with -ando (hablar → hablando) and replace -er or -ir with -iendo (comer → comiendo, vivir → viviendo). This is similar to English “am/is/are doing.”
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is in the middle of doing something?

cards.noteEn: Llegando is the -ando form of llegar. After a form of estar, it presents the arrival as an action in progress.

cards.answerEn: so; therefore (as part of así que)

cards.questionEn: How do you connect a situation to its result with “so”?
cards.answerEn: Use así que before the result.
cards.noteEn: Así que joins a cause or situation to what follows from it. The two words work together as one connector; translating así and que separately will not give the intended meaning.

example.es: Está lloviendo, así que llevo un paraguas.
example.en: It is raining, so I am carrying an umbrella.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of a result connector
It can say that something is expected or likely to happen.
cards.noteEn: Context decides between advice and expectation. Deberías descansar tells a person what they should do. El tren debería llegar pronto predicts what is expected to happen. In both uses, the following action stays in its dictionary form.
cards.questionEn: Besides giving advice, what can debería followed by a verb mean?

cards.noteEn: Spanish normally uses estar to say where a person or thing is. Estar is the verb's unchanged dictionary form.

example.en: I hope to be there tomorrow.

cards.noteEn: Ahí points to a place away from the speaker but normally not as distant as allí. The distinction varies by region and context.
Before a time span, en can measure how long from now it will be until a future event occurs. In another context, en plus a time span can instead say how long an activity takes to complete.

example.es: El tren llegará en diez minutos.
example.en: The train will arrive in ten minutes.

cards.promptEs: en + cantidad de tiempo (hasta un evento futuro)
cards.questionEn: How do you say how long from now it will be until something happens?
cards.answerEn: Use en before the amount of time.
cards.noteEn: With a future event, en plus a time span measures the interval from now until that event: llegará en diez minutos. With an activity that has a clear endpoint, the same pattern can instead say how long completion takes: lo terminó en una hora. The surrounding event tells which reading fits.

example.es: La película empezará en media hora.
example.en: The movie will start in half an hour.

cards.promptEs: estimaciones de tiempo · diálogo de copia de ficheros de Windows
cards.questionEn: Why does the visitor's arrival estimate swing between minutes, days, and seconds?
cards.answerEn: The visitor is personified as the author of a Windows file-copy dialog, so his unreliable arrival estimates imitate the wildly changing completion-time estimates produced while files are copied.
cards.noteEn: The official title text says the software could simply report a probably lost connection, but instead uses naive time-averaging that can preserve false hope with an enormous remaining-time estimate. The Spanish raster preserves the car scene and the same changing-time joke.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of en realidad (“actually”)

cards.noteEn: Use it to correct or qualify what someone may believe. It does not mean “currently”; Spanish normally uses actualmente for that meaning.
cards.questionEn: What expression means “actually” or “in fact” when correcting an impression?

example.es: Pensaba que era lunes, pero en realidad es martes.
example.en: I thought it was Monday, but it is actually Tuesday.

cards.answerEn: actually; in fact (as part of en realidad)

cards.noteEn: Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.answerEn: it will be; it will come to (a plural amount)
cards.noteEn: Serán is the future form of ser used with a plural amount. Spanish can match ser to plural time units, as in serán dos días, while natural English may use singular ‘it’: ‘it will be two days.’

example.en: It will be a three-hour trip.

cards.questionEn: How do you say what someone will do in Spanish?
cards.answerEn: Keep the action verb in its dictionary form and add a future ending such as -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, or -án.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. The ending identifies the person: sentir plus -á gives sentirá, and ver plus -á gives verá. A few common verbs change their stem, but use the same endings.

cards.answerEn: about; approximately (before a masculine plural amount)
cards.noteEn: Before a number, unos can make the quantity approximate. This differs from unos before an ordinary plural noun, where it usually means ‘some’ or ‘a few.’

example.en: We will take about twenty minutes.

cards.questionEn: How do you make a number sound approximate, like ‘about twenty minutes’?
cards.answerEn: Put unos or unas before the number.
cards.noteEn: Use unos before a masculine plural unit and unas before a feminine plural unit: unos veinte minutos, unas veinte personas. Here these words mean ‘about,’ rather than their ordinary ‘some’ meaning before a noun without a number.

cards.promptEs: orden afirmativa para tú: habla, come, escribe
cards.questionEn: How do you give one friend or familiar person a positive command?
cards.answerEn: Use the informal singular command form, often the same form used for “he” or “she” in the present.
cards.noteEn: For many regular verbs, -ar becomes -a and -er or -ir becomes -e: hablar becomes habla, comer becomes come, and escribir becomes escribe. Some common verbs are irregular or change their stem. Negative commands use a different form and are a separate pattern.
Del is the required contraction of de + el. It can mean “of the” or “from the,” depending on context.
In computing, diálogo or cuadro de diálogo is a small on-screen window that asks for information or reports status. This differs from diálogo meaning spoken conversation.

example.en: The dialog box shows the progress.

cards.answerEn: often no separate English word; links a noun to another noun that names its type or use
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses de between two nouns where English uses a noun directly before another noun. For example, una taza de café is ‘a coffee cup,’ and material de oficina is ‘office material.’
Here copia names the process of duplicating data, rather than one particular copy of an item.

example.es: La copia de datos tardó una hora.
example.en: Copying the data took an hour.

cards.noteEn: Visita is the present form of visitar for one person or thing described as he, she, or it. When the visitor goes to see specific people, Spanish normally uses a before them.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks a specific person as the object
cards.noteEn: Spanish generally places a before a specific person who receives a verb’s action. This “personal a” is not translated as a separate English word.

cards.promptEs: a + persona o expresión que se refiere a una persona
cards.questionEn: Why does Spanish sometimes put a before the person affected by an action?
cards.answerEn: Put a before a person—or a word such as alguien or nadie—when that person directly receives the action.
cards.noteEn: This a is called the personal a. It is common before a named or specific person, but person-denoting words such as alguien (“someone”) and nadie (“nobody”) also take it. English usually has no separate word for it. Before the masculine article el, a + el contracts to al.

cards.answerEn: some; a few (before a masculine plural noun)
cards.noteEn: Unos introduces an indefinite masculine plural group or amount. Use unas before a feminine plural noun.
